<meta>This page transitions from the formal dedication and signatures found on the previous page to the beginning of the Preface (Vorrede). ## Preface.

I can easily imagine, beloved reader, what kind of varied judgments this <term>treatise</term> <note>original: *Tractat*</note> by myself and my beloved <note>This refers to Johanna Eleonora von Merlau (1644–1724), the author’s wife and a prominent Pietist theologian who co-authored several works with him.</note> concerning the mystery of the <term>firstborn of all creation</term> <note>A central concept in Petersen’s theology, based on Colossians 1:15, often used to argue for the pre-existence of Christ’s soul and the eventual restoration of all things (Apokatastasis).</note> will be subjected to. I can see how not only the brawlers, who blindly and flatly blaspheme all rising divine truth, but also those who stiffly adhere to paternal dogmas and their own self-made *ideas* and refuse to leave them, will violently oppose it and reject it as a matter entirely foreign to them. 

Because I know, however, that it has always happened thus, and that not a single rising truth has ever existed without any contradiction—but rather, that through contradiction it has first spread far and wide and shown its strength and what it is capable of, so that its enemies finally had to surrender and yield to it—I am therefore not a little encouraged. I gain the courage to joyfully confess this highly praised God-Man as the firstborn of all creation, through whom both the old and new creation proceed, and to do so in the midst of the contradiction of all my ene...

<sig>)( )(</sig>
<meta>catchword: de [The word "enemies" (Feinde) is interrupted and would continue on the next page.]</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Johann Wilhelm Petersen introduces a controversial theological treatise written with his wife, anticipating and dismissing the inevitable criticism from traditionalists and skeptics. He argues that divine truth is often strengthened by the very opposition it faces.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Johann Wilhelm Petersen, Johanna Eleonora von Merlau, firstborn of all creation, theological controversy, Pietism, God-Man</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the sentence from the previous page, completing the word "enemies" (Feinde) and concluding the author's opening thought before moving into the second section of the preface. Petersen is establishing a parallel between the physical discoveries of the New World and his own theological "discoveries" in Scripture.</meta>

-mies to step forth, in the hope that, if not all, then many who are children of Wisdom <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 11:19 and Luke 7:35, often used by Pietists to refer to those spiritually enlightened enough to recognize divine truth.</note> shall be won over and overwhelmed by the power of this truth.

->§ 2.<-

As the two famous men **Columbus** and **Amerigo Vespucci** ventured out onto the vastness of the great sea under the favor of the great **God**, and newly found many islands and islets—which might have been well enough known to those living nearby for a long time—and told stories about them, many took it for a mere fable. Yet they finally had to believe it when the fruits and even some of the people who lived there were brought back. It is exactly the same today for those who find various wonders and secret, hidden things in the great sea of **Holy Scripture**. These things were already understood in former times by the first Christians and by the holy men of **God** in the Old Testament—from whom the wise pagans **Orpheus**, **Musaeus**, **Trismegistus**, **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and others received them, as **Augustine**, **Steuchus**, **Eugubinus** <note>Agostino Steuco (1497–1548), also known as Eugubinus, was an Italian humanist and scholar. His work argued that a single, primordial truth existed across all ancient philosophies.</note> testifies in his **Perennial Philosophy** <note>original: *Philosophia Perenni*. This refers to the concept that a core of universal truths has been handed down through the ages in various forms.</note>—but which have since fallen out of knowledge. Consequently, it now appears as if they were entirely newly invented. I say that those who have found such truth must allow themselves to be judged now this way, now that, as if they wished to preach new gods, and that they [speak] of such secrets...

<summary>Petersen compares the discovery of the Americas to his rediscovery of "hidden" scriptural truths, arguing that ancient wisdom (known to both early Christians and pagan sages) has been forgotten and is now mistakenly viewed as dangerous innovation.</summary>

May this holy **God-man**—**God the Word**, who became **flesh** and was exalted as such, and who sits in that same flesh at the right hand of the power of **God**—also be praised by us in his place forever and ever! # Explanation.

The Son of God / God the Word / Jesus Christ / is not called the beginning of God's creation <note>German: *Anfang der Creatur Gottes*</note> because he merely has precedence over all other creatures / or as if he were simply the first among them to be created. The Holy Fathers (for which reason we previously cited Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), a prominent theologian and bishop who defended the doctrine of the Trinity.</note>, specifically in the same oration in which he writes against the Arians <note>A group of early Christians who argued that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>) have called this matter a *condescension* <note>original Greek: *συνκατάβασιν* (*synkatabasis*), meaning a "stepping down" or stooping to a lower level.</note>, or the descending of God to the creatures. They said that for the sake of the creation of all things, God found a "tempering" <note>original: *Temperament*; used here in the sense of a moderation of intensity, like a dimmer switch for light.</note> in the First-born, so that the poor creature—who would otherwise be swallowed up by the eternal and infinite glow of God’s light, which no one can approach—might instead stand before Him in the tempered and moderate light of the First-born.

Philo Judæus <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used Greek philosophy to explain Hebrew scripture.</note> already testified to this in his own time: how God created the world through the *Word* <note>original Greek: *λόγον* (*Logos*)</note>, and how He communicated to the creature—who could not grasp it due to its own frailty—not His infinite power, but only as much as it was capable of receiving. "For since the divine powers surround him, and the creature being too weak to receive the magnitude—" <note>original Greek: *Ἐπεὶ γὰρ μὲν αἱ δυνάμεις περιβάλλουσι, Τὸ δ' ἀσθενέστερον ὄν, ἢ ὥστε δέξασθαι τὸ μέγε-*</note>

<meta>This page continues the author’s theological exploration of Christ’s identity. # Explanation.

The Firstborn—as well as the Only-begotten <term>Only-begotten: a traditional translation of the Greek *monogenēs*, referring to Christ as the unique, one-of-a-kind Son of God</term>—is the Son of the living God. However, insofar as Christ is called the **Son of Man**, He includes both His heavenly humanity and His lowly humanity assumed from Mary in such a manner of speaking. He speaks of His entire person and of everything that belongs to it, which is why He is also called the **Lamb of God**. He was appointed to this role by His Father from the beginning of the world, as the one through whom and in whom He could restore what sin had corrupted.

It is noteworthy that whenever the **Son of God** is spoken of in various places in the New Testament, He is immediately thereafter described using equivalent words—namely, as the **Son of Man**. For instance, when the disciples were once asked by the Lord what people were saying about who the **Son of Man** was, they answered that some said He was **John the Baptist**, others that He was **Elijah**, and some that He was **Jeremiah** or one of the prophets. <note>This refers to the biblical account in Matthew 16:13-17.</note> When Christ then wanted to know from them who *they* said He was, **Peter** answered in the name of the disciples: He was **Christ, the Son of the living God**. Christ confirmed this and at the same time added His blessing, praising Peter because "flesh and blood" <note>original: *Fleisch und Blut*. A biblical idiom meaning human reasoning or mortal power.</note> had not revealed this to him, but rather His Father in heaven.

<summary>This page explains the theological union of Christ’s titles, "Son of God" and "Son of Man," arguing they represent His complete person—encompassing both His divine origin and His earthly humanity. It cites Peter’s confession to show how these titles are used interchangeably to reveal Christ's true identity.</summary>

## 21.

I believe and confess that, although **Jesus Christ** has not cast off—nor will he ever cast off—the true **humanity** he took from **Mary**, he has nevertheless laid aside all the weaknesses of that humanity after his **Resurrection**. For this reason, he must be conceived of and believed in by us in his glorified **humanity**, which is exalted above all heavens. Thus, he is **omnipresent** <note>This refers to the doctrine of "Ubiquity," the belief that Christ's human nature, by virtue of its union with his divine nature, can be present everywhere.</note>—not only according to the **heavenly humanity** <note>original: "himmlische Menschheit." This likely refers to a specific theological concept where Christ is seen as having a divine or "celestial" human nature distinct from his earthly body.</note> which he possessed from the beginning, but also according to that glorified and exalted humanity which he received from **Mary**. 

This is especially true in the **Holy Supper** <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, wherein we—truly and not merely **symbolically** <note>original: "Bedeutungs-Weise." The author is rejecting the view that the bread and wine are only "signs" of a distant body.</note>—partake of both the **heavenly humanity** of the firstborn **God-man**, and the glorified **flesh and blood** taken from the **Mother of God** (which exists in an indissoluble union with his heavenly humanity). we receive these together with the **unchanged bread and wine** <note>This indicates a "Sacramental Union" or "Consubstantiation" view, where the bread remains bread even as it conveys the body of Christ, as opposed to the Catholic view where the bread's substance changes entirely.</note>, and thus we become partakers of his most blessed presence and fellowship.

Therefore, do not imagine Christ's humanity to be in a [specific] place, for after the resurrection it was translated into divinity. The divinity of Christ is not confined to a place; therefore, neither is his humanity. <note>original: "Indicat quod etiam secundum humanam naturam seu carnem... Divinitas Christi in loco non est, igitur neque ejus humanitas."</note>

prophets and patriarchs would have been without life from **God**, and consequently not blessed and glorified; or they also ate the flesh of the **Son of Man** and drank his blood, which must indeed have been present in the Old Testament as well, since they drank it then. For, according to the testimony of the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 10, they ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink with us, which flowed from the rock, which was **Christ**; <note>referencing 1 Corinthians 10:3-4, where Paul identifies the rock that followed the Israelites in the desert as Christ.</note> whom the unbelievers in the wilderness tempted, but the believers enjoyed for their salvation. This would have given them ample cause for praise and thanksgiving throughout eternity. We have already treated this in various places above, to which we refer the reader. But now we wish to take to heart together the great majesty and the nobility of our origin, so far as our faith allows. According to our first forefather <term>Stamm-Vater (progenitor or ancestral father)</term>, Adam, we have only a poor lineage to show. Many among the "great ones" of the world are accustomed to take comfort in such a lineage, tracing their old family line back quite far; they delight if they can prove that they descend from this or that pagan king or commander, or some other war hero or ancient family. 

Yet, even if such things are fully proven, they demonstrate nothing else but that their ancestors were long ago great sinners, and that their lineage—as **God** speaks—is from the land of the Canaanites, with a father from the Amorites and a mother from the Hittites <note>A reference to Ezekiel 16:3, where God describes the spiritual ancestry of a faithless Jerusalem as being rooted in pagan nations rather than a holy heritage.</note>.

Mysteries. It is permissible to know that He was born; it is not permissible to dispute how He was born. I may not deny the former; to inquire into the latter is a source of dread. For if Paul calls those things he heard, when caught up to the third heaven, *inexpressible*: how can we express the secret of the Father’s begetting <note>original: "paternæ generationis arcanum," referring to the theological concept of the "eternal generation" of the Son from the Father</note>, which we could neither perceive nor hear?

If the peace of Christ is higher than all reason, how then should such a great birth not be above all reason? Lay your hand upon your mouth; the divine mysteries must not be scrutinized. One can and may well know that He was born. I must not deny the former, but to scrutinize the latter is dangerous. For as Paul, when he was caught up into the third heaven, heard unspeakable words that no human can utter, how should we then be able to express the mystery of the divine birth of the Son from the Father? Which we can neither feel nor hear. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and influential theologian known as "The Theologian" for his work on the Trinity.</note> also writes of this very thoughtfully in *Oration 1, on the begetting of the Son, page 112.* Let us venerate the begetting of God with silence. Let it be a great thing for you to understand that He was begotten; but by what manner, that is not even for the angels to think upon, much less do we permit it to you. Do you want me to tell you how? It is known to the Father who begot, and to the Son who was begotten; that which is beyond this is obscured by a cloud, and [from] your eyes—

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "Firstborn" (Primogenitus) concept. The previous page established that the "Only-begotten" refers to the Son's eternal existence within the Trinity, while the "Firstborn" refers to the God-Man acting as a bridge to creation. This page now seeks historical validation for this view from the Early Church Fathers, specifically Athanasius.</meta>

<page-num>293</page-num>
<sig>T 3</sig>

*Timothy.* Has something of this mystery of the **Firstborn** not been seen and recognized in the Holy Antiquity of the early Christian churches?

*Paul.* Yes, for thus writes Saint Athanasius—to whom the Athanasian Creed <term>original: *Symbolum Athanasii*—a statement of Christian belief focused on the Trinity and the nature of Christ.</term> is attributed, and who was a mighty champion against the Arians <term>original: *Arrianer*—followers of Arius, who argued that Jesus was a created being rather than eternally God.</term> for the divinity of the Son of God—in his third sermon against the Arians on page 211:

<note>original Latin: "Omnibus liquet, Filium Dei, non propter se quasi & ipse creatum quiddam esset, neque quia cognatam essentiam affinemque habebat cum rebus creatitiis, nomine PRIMOGENITI vocatum esse, sed quia, quum primum conderet creaturas, attemperavit, & demisit se ad earum rationem, ut illæ ad essentiam pervenire possent, quæ alioquin non tulissent ejus naturam, INDILUTUM scilicet ET PATRIUM SPLENDOREM, nisi pro Patris sui in homines amore, accommodans sese eas arripuisset, & ad existendi facultatem protraxisset."</note>
"It is clear to everyone that the Son of God was not called by the name of the **FIRSTBORN** for his own sake—as if he himself were also some kind of created thing, or because he possessed an essence related or akin to created things—but because, when he first established the creatures, he tempered and lowered himself to their capacity, so that they might be able to attain to existence. Otherwise, they could not have endured his nature, which is the **UNDILUTED AND PATERNAL SPLENDOR**, unless out of his Father's love for mankind, he had accommodated himself, taken hold of them, and brought them forth into the capacity for existing."

<note>original Latin: "Altera deinde causa est hujus nominis, quod, ubi se denuo creatis condescendendo attemperat, ipsa creatura in jus filiorum adoptata sit, ita ut per omnia ejus PRIMOGENITUS efficeretur, tum in creando, tum in inferendo se ipsum pro omnibus in mundum."</note>
"The second reason for this name is that, when he again tempers himself by condescending to the created ones, the creature itself is adopted into the right of children, so that in all things he might be made its **FIRSTBORN**, both in creating and in bringing himself into the world on behalf of all."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Timotheus and Paulus. Paulus. No. For as the Holy Fathers constantly write concerning Arius and the Arians / Arius always had this saying in his mouth: *there was a time when the Son was not* <note>original Latin: "erat tempus, ubi non erat Filius"</note> / for this reason Nicephorus Callistus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos (c. 1256–1335), the last of the Greek ecclesiastical historians.</note> in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, Chapter VIII, page 366, records the Greek words he is said to have used: <term>The Word of God was not always</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἀεὶ ἦν ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγος"; Latin: "Non semper erat Dei Verbum"</note>. The Word of God has not existed at all times / or was not always. Likewise, it can be seen from his own letter to Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Nicomedia, a 4th-century bishop and primary supporter of Arius.</note>: <term>We say that [the Word] is from things that do not exist</term> <note>original Greek: "εἴπαμεν, ὅτι ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἐστίν"; Latin: "Dicimus, quod (Verbum) ex non existentibus sit"</note>. For this reason, He is in no way to be placed among the number of creatures / as if He were the first creature / but rather He is the <term>firstborn of all creation</term> <note>original Greek: "πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως"</note> / through whom all creatures have their beginning and were created (Colossians I).

Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan and a fierce opponent of Arianism.</note> has a very well-regarded passage on this in Book I of *On the Faith*, Chapter V, concerning the eternal Son of God / which powerfully presses the word <term>was, was, was, was</term> <note>original Greek: "ἦν, ἦν, ἦν, ἦν"</note> from the first chapter of John against Arius / and on page 101 writes thus: *When you have said "Father," you have also [spoken of] his...* <note>original Latin: "Cum Patrem dixeris, ejus etiam"; the text cuts off here as it reaches the end of the page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Paulus's defense of the eternal nature of the Son against the Arian heresy. <sig>X 3</sig>

You have designated Him "Son," because no one is a son to himself. Therefore, neither is the Son without the Father, nor can the Father be without the Son. Always, therefore, the Father exists, and always the Son. For "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; this was in the beginning with God." <note>John 1:1-2</note> HE WAS, it says, with God—WAS, WAS, WAS, WAS—behold! *four times "was"*. <note>The author is highlighting that the repetition of the imperfect tense "was" (Latin: *erat*) in the opening of John’s Gospel emphasizes continuous existence in the past, rather than a point of creation.</note> Where then does the ungodly man <note>Referring to Arius.</note> find that he "was not"? Elsewhere also, John says in his Epistle <note>1 John 1:1</note> "that which was in the beginning"; the word "was" is extended indefinitely. Whatever you might think of, the *Son was*. Indeed, our fisherman (John) <note>John the Apostle, traditionally characterized as the "fisherman" to contrast his humble origins with his profound theological insights.</note> excluded all heresies with this short chapter. For that which was in the beginning is not enclosed by time, nor preceded by any beginning. Therefore, let Arius be silent.

But Arius—as it stands in his letter to Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Nicomedia, the influential bishop who supported Arius.</note>—contradicted Alexander <note>Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, who first condemned Arius’s teachings.</note>, who had said that the Father has always been, and the Son has always been, and he expressly mentioned there that he does not hold with Alexander, nor agree with him: <term>since we do not agree with him when he says publicly: God is always, the Son is always; at once Father, at once Son; the Son co-exists with God without being begotten; He is always-begotten, He is unbegotten-begotten; neither in thought nor in any moment does God precede the Son; always God, always Son; the Son is from God himself.</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐπειδὴ οὐ συμφωνοῦμεν αὐτῷ δημοσίᾳ λέγοντι, ἀεὶ ὁ Θεὸς, ἀεὶ ὁ υἱὸς, ἅμα πατὴρ, ἅμα υἱὸς, συνυπάρχει ἀγεννήτως ὁ υἱὸς τῷ Θεῷ, ἀειγενής ἐστι, ἀγεννητογενής ἐστι, οὔτε ἐπινοίᾳ οὔτε ἀτόμῳ, τινὶ προάγει ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ υἱοῦ, ἀεὶ Θεὸς, ἀεὶ υἱὸς, ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ ὁ υἱὸς"</note>

That is: <term>Since we do not agree with Alexander who says publicly: Always God, always Son, at the same time Father, at the same time Son. The Son co-exists with the unbegotten God, always</term> <note>original Latin: "Quoniam non concordamus Alexandro publice dicenti: Semper Deus, semper Filius, simul Pater, simul Filius. <meta>This page continues the argument from page 328, where Paulus uses the analogy of an orator and his book to explain how Wisdom can be both eternal within God and "created" or "brought forth" for the sake of the world.</meta>

Wisdom herself says: The Lord created (or possessed) me as the beginning of his ways <note>original Latin: "Dominus creavit (aut possedit) me initium viarum suarum." This is a reference to Proverbs 8:22, a central text in historical debates regarding whether Christ, as Wisdom, was created or eternal.</note>. The Architect full of wisdom, indeed the very fountain of wisdom, brought forth from himself Wisdom itself; indeed, hear what Wisdom says: I, Wisdom, founded the earth, and prepared the heavens with prudence <note>original Latin: "Ego sapientia fundavi terram, puravi cœlos prudentia."</note>. Therefore, since time does not arise except from days, and days from light, and light only from heaven, and heaven has not arisen except from Wisdom—and since before heaven time does not exist at all—it follows that Wisdom has always existed. Thus, Wisdom was created (or emanated) in the way we have described: as a book of secrets for a most wise Orator. 

The matter is briefly this, as Arnobius <note>Likely Arnobius the Younger, a 5th-century author whose works were often studied for their perspectives on the nature of Christ.</note> presents it: just as the oration or the poem <note>original Latin: "Carmen"</note> that I have composed in my mind must have existed within me before I produced it, and also remains within me after I have produced it; so too must Wisdom—which is the God-humanity of the Firstborn of all creation—have proceeded from the infinite Godhead. It came forth as something distinct from that from which it originated, and yet it remains within Him. At the same time, it must be conceived as something less than the one who spoke it, since the one who speaks the poem is more than the poem itself, and his inner, invisible nature becomes visible through the poem. 

Concerning the Holy Trinity, Arnobius writes on folio 526 as follows: "From that which God is, from that also is the Father, and from that is His Son: for He began to have nothing in Himself by substance <note>original Latin: "per substantiam"</note> which He did not have before. For He was always with the Vir-" <meta>The word continues on the next page as "Virtute" (Virtue/Power).</meta>

<summary>This page uses the writings of Arnobius to explain the eternal nature of Wisdom (Christ), arguing that just as a poem exists in a poet's mind before it is written, Wisdom existed in God before the creation of the world.</summary>

**Q. 1. Who is the <term>Firstborn of all creation</term>?** <note>original: "Erstgebohrne aller Creatur." This is a reference to Colossians 1:15, a key verse used in historical theology to describe Christ’s status and pre-existence before the world was made.</note>

**R.** He is Jesus Christ / yesterday and today / and the same also for eternity. Hebrews 13:8.

**Q. 2. Has this Jesus Christ / the heavenly <term>God-Man</term> <note>original: "Gott-Mensch." This term refers to the union of divine and human natures in the person of Christ.</note> / already existed from the beginning?**

**R.** Yes / for that is why He is named JESUS Christ / yesterday and today / and therefore it is written: The Lord possessed me at the beginning of His ways / before He made anything / I was there. Proverbs 8:22. <note>In this period, the "Wisdom" speaking in Proverbs 8 was almost universally interpreted by theologians as the pre-existent Christ.</note>

**Q. 3. What other names are given to this highly praised God-Man in Holy Scripture?**

**R.** This Firstborn of all creation is called / God / the Word / and the Wisdom of God. Colossians 1:15. John 1:1. Proverbs 8:12, 22, 23, 24, and following. Chapter 9:1. Luke 11:49.

**Q. 4. How do you prove / that all of these are the same?**

**R.** By this / because that which is written of Wisdom in Holy Scripture / is also said of God the Word / and what is said of God / the Word / is also said of the Firstborn of all creations.

**Q. 18.** But should one indeed be able to clearly prove from the **Old Testament** / that **Christ Jesus** / yesterday and today / was the **God-man**?

**R.** Yes, certainly / for the first man was indeed created before the Fall / according to the **image of God** / which was Christ / so the original image must have already been the **God-man** at that time. Genesis 1:27.

**Q. 19.** Is there another passage regarding this?

**R.** Yes / for Jacob wrestled with **God** and men / so the **God-man** with whom he wrestled must have been present there. Genesis 32:28.

**Q. 20.** Is there also a verse about this in the **New Testament**?

**R.** Yes / for there Christ is called the **second Adam** / the **Lord from heaven** / who was made into a **life-giving spirit**. 1 Corinthians 15:45. John 6:63.

**Q. 30. Do we then partake in the Holy Supper <note>The German "Abendmahl" literally translates to "Evening Meal," the standard term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> of the body of Christ / which was broken for us / and his blood / which was poured out for us?**

**R.** Yes / for just as GOD redeemed his congregation with his blood / so we also eat and drink in the Holy Supper his glorified body / and glorified blood / which was born of Mary / and united itself with GOD / the Word.
->Acts 20:28. <note>original: "Actor. XX. 28." referring to the Latin *Actorum Apostolorum*.</note><-

**Q. 31. If we then worthily eat and drink the flesh and blood of the Son of GOD / what benefit do we have from it?**

**R.** Christ speaks of it thus: Whoever eats my flesh / and drinks my blood / remains in me / and I in him / and has eternal life / and I will raise him up on the Last Day.
->John 6:54, 56.<-

**Q. 32. Will we then / as many of us as have believed / and been born again / also be like the glorified body of Christ on the Last Day of this world?**

**R.** Yes / for just as we have borne the image of the earthly / so shall we also bear the image of the heavenly / for flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God / nor does the perishable <term>perishable: that which is subject to decay or death; in German "Verweßliche."</term> inherit the imperishable.
->1 Corinthians 15:49, 50.<-
